sections.section_title: Introduction to Daily Worship in Śiva Temples
sections.content: The daily worship of Śiva in a shrine is given in several Āgama texts like Kāmika, Ajita and Kāraṇa, and also in manuals like Śivārcana-candrikā, śaivāgama-candrikā, Sivāgamasāra and Iśāna-śiva-guru-deva-padhati. The following is more or less a standard procedure adopted in the Śiva-temples in South India. The sequences are drawn from. Arcanāprakāśa (Manonmani-granthamālā - 1962, edited by Talakādu Kṛṣṇa-Dīkṣita), which is a compilation from different Śaivāgama-texts.
sections.summary: This section introduces the topic of daily worship (Nityārcanā) of Śiva in South Indian temples. It lists the primary scriptural sources, which are Āgama texts (Kāmika, Ajita, Kāraṇa) and manuals (Śivārcana-candrikā, etc.). It specifies that the procedure described is based on 'Arcanāprakāśa', a compilation from various Śaivāgama texts edited by Talakādu Kṛṣṇa-Dīkṣita.

sections.section_title: The Priest's Entry and Preliminary Rites
sections.content:
I. The priest (ācārya), finsishing his ablutions and other daily obligatory rituals, comes to the temple, and washing his feet before entering the temple premises. He enters through the main door, reciting
ॐ भद्रं कर्णेभिः श्रुणुयाम देवा
भद्रं पश्येमाक्षभिर्यजत्राः ।
स्थिरैरङ्‌गैस्तुष्टवांसस्तनूभिः
व्यशेम देवहितं यदायुः ॥
He offers brief worship to Gaņeśa and Durgā, installed at the main door., He then prostarates before the shrine at the doorway or in the courtyard in front of the altar-seat (bali-pītha). He bows before the flag-post (dhvaja-stambha), the image of the crouching bull (vṛśabha), and the icons of the door-guardians (dvārapāla). He opens the door of the sanctum, reciting 'om astrāya phat' (astra-mantra), He cleans the sanctum and the porch, and attends to the lights within the sanctum.
According to śaivāgama-sāra, the cleaning of the sanctum must be done with the broom made out of the coconut leaves (nārikela-taru-parņakāsthaih vinirmitam') with pañca-gavya, and with clean water, by the priest himself ('svayam eva tu deśikah') Kāmikāgama allows the priest's attendant (paricāraka) to attend to the cleaning of the area till the bali-pitha, outside the sanctum. Ceremonial cleaning involves mārjana, prokşaņa and gomaya-vilepana, viz. sweeping, sprinkling and application of cow-dung paste.
अथ महादेवस्य नित्यार्चनाविधिं व्याख्यास्यामः। आचार्यः प्रातर्विनिद्रः शौचाचमनस्नानवस्त्रोपवीतविभूतिरुद्राक्षमालिका-धारणसन्ध्योपासनादिकृतनित्यकर्मा देवस्थानं गत्वा द्वारदेशे पादप्रक्षालनं विधाय ॐ भद्रं कर्णेभिरित मन्त्रेणान्तः प्रविष्य महाद्वारे नृत्तगणेशं दुर्गा च प्रणम्य ध्यायेत्-
पाशङ्‌कुशापूपकुठारदन्तचञ्चत्कराक्लृप्तवराङ्गुलीयकम्।
पीतप्रभं कल्पतरोरधस्थं भजामि नृत्तोपपदं गणेशम् ॥
कालां स्फालां कटाक्षैः अरिकुलभयदां मौलिबद्धेन्दुरेखाम्
शङ्ख चक्रं कृपाणं त्रिशिखमपि करैः उद्वहन्तीं त्रिणेत्राम्।
सिंहस्कन्धाधिरूढां त्रिभुवनमखिलं तेजसा पूरयत्नीं
ध्यायेदुर्गा जयाख्यां त्रिदशपरिवृतां सेवितां सिद्धिकामैः ॥
इति ध्यात्वा पञ्चोपचारैः सम्पूज्य
गोपुरद्वारबाह्ये बलिपीठस्य बाह्ये वा विमानस्य नमस्कारं कुर्यात् ।
ततः बलिपीठस्य ध्यजस्तम्भस्यापि नमस्कारं कृत्वा अन्तः प्रवेशे शिवदर्शने च शिवार्चनतत्फलसिद्धिलाभे ।
देह्यभ्यनुज्ञां भगवन् प्रसन्नस्त्त्वत्पादपद्मप्रणताय मह्यम् ।
वन्दे वृषभदेवाय सितवर्णस्वरूपिणे ।
तीक्ष्णशृ‌ङ्गाय तुङ्‌ङ्गाय वेदपादाय नन्दिने ।॥
इति वृषभं सम्प्रार्थ्य बलिपीठाग्रदेशे साष्टाङ्‌गा प्रणम्य प्रदक्षिणक्रमेण मूलमन्त्रमनुस्मरन् मुखमण्टपमासाद्य
नमोस्तु द्वारपालेभ्यः शिवस्य परमात्मनः ।
भवतामनुकूलेन नित्यपूजां करोम्यहम्॥
इति द्वारपालान् प्रणम्य, स्नपनमण्डपमुपगम्य, वृषभाग्रे देवदेवं नमस्कृत्य
देवदेव जगन्नााथ चन्द्रार्धकृतशेखर ।
भगवन् तव सेवार्थमनुज्ञां दातुमर्हसि ।।
इति मूलदेवतां प्रणम्य ॐ हः अस्त्राय फट् इति मन्त्रेण देवद्वारकवाटमुद्घाटय यथासम्भवं बलिपीठान्तं आलय-शुद्धिसम्मार्जनादींश्च कारयित्वा उद्दीप्यस्वेति दीपप्रज्वलनं कारयित्वा पूजोपकरणपात्राणाञ्चोक्तद्रव्यैः शुद्धिं कारयेत् ।
sections.summary: This section outlines the initial actions of the priest (ācārya) upon arriving at the temple. After personal purification, the priest enters reciting a Vedic hymn, worships Gaṇeśa and Durgā at the main door, and pays respects to the bali-pīṭha, dhvaja-stambha, vṛśabha (Nandi), and dvārapālas. He then opens the sanctum using the astra-mantra and performs cleaning rituals, which involve sweeping, sprinkling with pañca-gavya, and applying cow-dung paste. Variations in who performs the cleaning (priest or attendant) based on different Āgamas are noted.

sections.content:
II. Having duly entered the sanctum, he sanctifies the water that is to be used for worship, and sprinkles all the vessels and articles employed during worship with that water.
ततः सामान्यार्घ्यपात्रं ॐ हां शिवास्त्राय नमः इति मन्त्रेण प्रक्षाल्य बिन्दुस्थानस्त्रवदमृततया भाविते (शुद्धजलेन) गन्ध तोयेन ॐ हां हृदयाय वौषड् इत्यापूर्य ॐ हां हृदयाय नमः इति सप्तवारमाभिमन्त्र्य ॐ हां कवचाय नमः इत्यवकुण्ठ्य गन्धपुष्पादिभिरभ्यर्च्य धेनुमुद्रां प्रदर्थ्य तदम्भसा सर्वाणि पुजोपकरणानि आत्मानं च सम्प्रोक्षयेत्।
sections.summary: Inside the sanctum, the priest sanctifies the water intended for worship (sāmānya-arghya). He does this by washing a vessel with the Śivāstra mantra, filling it with pure, scented water, chanting the hṛdaya mantra seven times, and performing protective mudrās. This consecrated water is then sprinkled over all worship articles and on himself for purification.

sections.section_title: Permission from Kṣetrapāla and Worship of Guardian Deities
sections.content:
III. (a) He next seeks for the permission of Kṣetrapāla, offering arghya. He proceeds to eschew the triple-obstacles, and to worship the guardian deities.
अनुज्ञार्थं क्षेत्रपालसन्निधिमुपगम्य सामान्यार्घ्यजलेन द्वारमस्त्रेण सम्प्रोक्ष्य
द्वारदक्षिणपाश्वें- ॐ हां वीरगणपतये नमः।
वामपवें- ॐ हां शक्तिगणपतये नमः।
मध्ये - ॐ हां महालक्ष्म्यै नमः ।
द्वारवामे ॐ हां धर्मशक्तिभ्यो नमः।
द्वारदक्षिणे - ॐ हां धर्मद्वारपालाय नमः।
द्वारोत्तरे ॐ हां अधर्मद्वारपालय नमः।
इति द्वारपूजां विधाय
(b) He sprinkles the arghya-water on the main deity (linga) in the sanctum, and remotues the old flowers.
अथ त्रिविधविघ्नानुत्सार्य अर्घ्यजलेन बिम्बं सम्प्रोक्ष्य निर्माल्यं विसृज्य ॐ क्षं क्षेत्रपालाय नमः इति मूलेन बिम्बशुद्धि कृत्वा ॐ हां आधारशक्त्यै नमः इत्याधारशक्तिं सम्पूज्य
(c) He preliminarily cleans the deity and worships ādhāra-śakti, and other divinities of the pedestal. This is a part of the worship of Kṣetra-pāla.
ॐ हां अनन्तासनाय नमः ।
ॐ हां धर्माय नमः ।
ॐ हां ज्ञानाय नमः।
ॐ हां वैराग्याय नमः।
ॐ हां ऐश्वर्याय नमः।
ॐ हां पद्माय नमः
इति सम्पूज्य
ॐ क्षं क्षेत्रपालासनाय नमः।
ॐ क्षं क्षेत्रपालमूर्तये नमः।
ॐ क्षं क्षेत्रपालाय नमः।
(d) Then follows the worship of Kṣetra-pāla in detali:
"नग्नरूपं त्रिणेत्रं च सर्पाभरणभूषितम्।
रत्नकुडलसंयुक्तं शिरोमालाविभूषितम् ।।
खड्गं शूलं कपालं च डमरुं भीमदंष्ट्रकम्।
बिभ्राणं शुनकारूढं क्षेत्रपालमहं भजे ॥
ॐ हां हर्हा हूं हैं हौं क्षं क्षेत्रपालाय नमः ॥
क्षेत्रस्य पतिना वयं इति मन्त्रेणावाह्य स्थापनादि मुद्राः मूर्तिमन्त्रेण प्रदर्थ्य अभ्य‌ङ्गादिभिरभिषिच्यालङ्ङ्कत्य पञ्चब्रह्मसहितषङङ्ङ्ग क्षेत्रपालमूलेन विन्यसेत्।
तद्यथा
ॐ हों क्षं क्षेत्रपालाय ईशानमूनें नमः ।
ॐ हें क्षं क्षेत्रपालाय तत्पुरुषावक्त्राय नमः ।
ॐ ह्रीं क्षं क्षेत्रपालाय अघोरहृदयाय नमः ।
ॐ हां क्षं क्षेत्रपालाय सद्योजातपादाभ्यां नमः।
ॐ हां क्षं क्षेत्रपालाय हृदयाय नमः ।
ॐ हूं क्षं क्षेत्रपालाय शिखायै नमः ।
ॐ हूं क्ष क्षेत्रपालाय शिखायै नमः ।
ॐ हौं हौं क्षं क्षेत्रपालाय कवचाय नमः।
ॐ हौं क्षं क्षेत्रपालाय नेत्रत्रयाय नमः।
ॐ हं क्षं क्षेत्रपालाय अस्त्राय नमः ॥
अथ धेनुपद्मलिङ्ङ्गस्त्रमहामुद्राः प्रदर्थ्य दध्यन्न लाजां वा निवेद्यधूपदीपार्ष्याणि दत्त्वा प्रार्थयेत् ।
"स्वामिन् सर्वजनान् भूमौ रक्षितुं क्षेत्रपालक।
शिवपूजाविधानार्थे मुद्रादण्डं प्रदेहि मे ॥
इति सम्प्रार्थ्य निरोधार्घ्य दत्वा नमस्कारमुद्रां प्रदर्थ्य अङ्‌कुशमुद्रया मुद्रदण्डं गृह्णीयात् ।
sections.summary: The priest seeks permission from Kṣetrapāla (the guardian of the site) to begin the worship. This involves worshipping various guardian deities at the doorway, such as Vīragaṇapati and Mahālakṣmī. The main deity (liṅga) is then sprinkled with arghya water, and the old flowers (nirmālya) are removed. The pedestal's divinities, including Ādhāra-śakti, Ananta, Dharma, etc., are worshipped as part of the Kṣetrapāla ritual. A detailed meditation (dhyāna) and mantra worship for Kṣetrapāla follows, involving invocation, nyāsa with Pañcabrahmamantras, and offerings. The priest concludes by ritually receiving the 'mudrādaṇḍa' (staff of authority) from Kṣetrapāla.

sections.content:
IV. The priest then goes to the apartment where the processional deity had been put to bed the previous night, and formally wakes him up along with his consort. The two deities are then brought to the customary seat near the sanctum.
अथ शयनालयद्वारमुपगम्य शिवशक्तिनिद्रोन्मीलनार्थे द्वारपार्श्वे रुद्रगणिकाभिः नृत्तगीतवाद्यादिकं कारयित्वा द्वारपूजां विद्ध्यात् ।
ॐ हां गं गणपतये नमः इति दक्षिणे
ॐ हां सं सरस्वत्यै नमः इति उत्तरे
ॐ हां श्री महालक्ष्यै नमः इति मध्ये
ॐ हां गं गङ्‌‌गायै नमः इति दक्षिणपार्श्वे
ॐ हां यं यमुनायै नमः इति वामपवें
ॐ हां नं नर्मदायै नमः इति मध्ये
ॐ हों कं कन्यापयोष्ण्यै नमः
ॐ हां सिं सिन्धवे नमः इति ऊध्वें
ॐ हां तुं तुङ्‌ङ्गभद्रायै नमः
ॐ हां चं चन्द्रभागायै नमः इति अधः
इति द्वारपूजां विधाय प्रार्थयेत्।
वेदान्तवेद्योऽखिलविश्वमूर्ते विभो विरूपाक्ष विशेषवेद्य।
विश्वेश्वराशेषविशेषमूर्ते कवाटमुद्घाटय कालकाल ॥
इति सम्प्रार्थ्य कवाटोद्घाटनं कुर्यात् ।
अथ विघ्नत्रयं निवार्य अन्तः प्रविश्य अर्योदकेनास्त्रेण मञ्चावृतिरोधानपटं सम्प्रोक्ष्य वर्मणाऽभ्युक्ष्य अर्घ्यपात्रं मञ्चोपरि निक्षिप्य अर्घ्यजलेन अस्त्रेण मूर्ति सम्प्रोक्ष्य, उत्तिष्ठ ब्राह्मणस्पत इति मन्त्रेण देवं देवीं च उत्थाप्य निर्माल्यं विसृज्य पादहस्तशुद्ध्यर्थे अस्त्रेण उदकं दत्वा स्नानार्थमूलेन अर्योदकेन सम्प्रोक्ष्य नववस्त्रगन्धमाल्याभिरलङकृत्य मूलब्रह्माङ्‌गमन्त्रैः सम्पूज्य चित्रान्नं लाजां वा निवेद्य धूपदीपार्घ्यताम्बूलानि दत्वा
नमः शिवाय साम्बाय लोकानुग्रहहेतवे ।
भुक्तिमुक्तिकृते तुभ्यं पञ्चकृत्यविधानतः ॥
कृपया मम विश्वेश नित्यापूजार्थमादरात्।
अनुज्ञां देहि भक्तिञ्च तव पादाब्जपूजने ।।
इति सम्प्रार्थ्य
देवं शिबिकामारोप्य भद्रं कर्णेति मन्त्रतः सर्वविध वाद्योपचारपरिजनैश्च सार्धं लिङ्गसन्निधिमुपगम्य पुष्पेण उद्भवमुद्रया लिङ्‌गे संयोज्य यथास्थाने मूर्ति संस्थाप्य पञ्चोपचारेण सम्पूज्य उषः कालार्चनं कुर्यात् ।
sections.summary: The priest proceeds to the 'śayanālaya' (sleeping chamber) to wake the processional deities (Śiva and Śakti). This involves music and dance performances, worship of deities at the chamber door (Gaṇapati, Sarasvatī, Mahālakṣmī, and various sacred rivers), and a prayer to Śiva to 'open the door'. Inside, the deities are ceremonially woken, adorned with new clothes and garlands, offered food and other items, and then brought in a palanquin (śibikā) to their place near the main sanctum for the early dawn worship (Uṣaḥ-kāla-arcana).

sections.content:
Worship is prescribed to be done three or six times: morning, noon and night ('prātar-madhyāhna-rātrī ca hime kālās trayahj smṛtāh') Texts also permit worship tow times, once during the day and once during night ('divārātram dvayam smrtam') or once only at noon ('ekam madhyāhna kālas syāt). When it is śat-kāla-pūjā (six times): (1) uśahkāla (early dawn, before sunrise), (2) pūrvāhņa (morning), (3) madhyāhna (noon), (4) pradośa (late afternoon), (5) sāyamkāla (evning ) and (6) ardha-yāma (late night).
What follows is the sequence of uśah-kāla pūjā:
sections.summary: This brief section discusses the prescribed frequency of worship. It can be performed three times (morning, noon, night), six times (ṣaṭ-kāla-pūjā), twice (day and night), or just once (at noon). The six time slots are listed: uṣaḥkāla (early dawn), pūrvāhṇa (morning), madhyāhna (noon), pradoṣa (late afternoon), sāyaṃkāla (evening), and ardha-yāma (late night). The text then states it will detail the uṣaḥ-kāla pūjā.

sections.content:
V. Agrodaka:
The priest proceeds to collect the water that is required for worship from a river or tank. He goes there in a procession in which five musical instruments (pañca-vādya) are sounded, and collects water reciting Rudra-sūkta, in five or nine vessels. The five musical instruments are kāhali, pațaha, śamkha, bheri and jaya-ghanțikā. This must be done early in the morning each day ('udaye rātryante vā jalam haret') The water so collected must be brought to the temple carried on the back of an elephant or on the head of the priest. The pot containing the water must be decorated with flowers; and must be honoured by umbrella and fly-whisks. And Vedic hymns must be recited along with the musical instruments. The procession goes round the temple ('dhāma-pradaksiņam kṛtvā') before the water is placed in front of the deity in the sanctum.
sections.summary: Agrodaka is the ritual of collecting fresh water for the day's worship. This is done early in the morning from a river or tank. The priest goes in a procession with five musical instruments (pañca-vādya), collects the water in several vessels while reciting the Rudra-sūkta, and brings it back to the temple with honors (on an elephant or his head, with umbrellas and fly-whisks). The procession circumambulates the temple before the water is placed in the sanctum.

sections.content: The first elaborate worship of the day is known as Prātah-kāla-pūjā. This involves purification of oneself (ātma-śuddhi), purification of the sat (asana-śuddhi), purification of the elements (bhūta-śuddhi), internal worship (antaryāga), purifications of the implements and articles of worship (dravya-śuddhi) and effectivization of mantras to be used in worship.
sections.summary: This introduces the main morning worship, Prātaḥ-kāla-pūjā. It is a comprehensive ritual involving a series of purifications: of the self (ātma-śuddhi), the seat (āsana-śuddhi), the elements (bhūta-śuddhi), and the worship articles (dravya-śuddhi), as well as internal worship (antaryāga) and mantra purification.

sections.content: [The content for this section spans multiple pages and subsections (a to j) detailing various purification rites like ātma-śuddhi, ācamana, prāṇāyāma, śiva-hasta-bhāvanā, sakali-karaṇa, bhūta-śuddhi, antaryāga, sthāna-śuddhi, and dravya-śuddhi. It includes numerous Sanskrit mantras and procedural descriptions for purifying the priest's body, mind, elements, worship space, and materials, preparing them for the divine invocation.]
sections.summary: This extensive section details the series of purification rituals (śuddhi) that form the foundation of the Prātaḥ-kāla-pūjā. It begins with the purification of the priest's seat (āsana) and self (ātma-śuddhi), which includes ceremonial sipping of water (ācamana) and breath control (prāṇāyāma). It progresses to esoteric practices like visualizing the divine hand of Śiva (śiva-hasta-bhāvanā) and divinizing one's own body through mantra placement (sakali-karaṇa). This is followed by bhūta-śuddhi, a complex visualization process of dissolving the physical elements of the body and recreating a divine one fit for worship. Antaryāga, or internal worship, involves mentally performing the entire ritual within one's heart. Finally, the physical space (sthāna-śuddhi) and all the articles to be used in the worship (dravya-śuddhi) are purified and consecrated with mantras.

sections.section_title: Preparation of Arghya, Pañca-gavya, and Pañcāmṛta
sections.content: [This subsection, part of the larger Dravya-śuddhi, details the preparation of three key offerings: (i) arghya (respectful water offering), (ii) pañca-gavya (mixture of five cow products), and (iii) pañcāmṛta (mixture of five nectars). It includes the specific mantras for consecrating each ingredient and the final mixtures, along with the visualization of associated deities.]
sections.summary: This part focuses on preparing and consecrating key liquid offerings. Arghya (honorable water) is prepared in different vessels for specific purposes. Pañca-gavya, a mixture of milk, curd, ghee, cow urine, and cow dung, is prepared in a specially drawn nine-chambered diagram (navakoṣṭha), with each ingredient being consecrated with specific mantras and associated with a face of Śiva. Similarly, Pañcāmṛta (five nectars: milk, curd, ghee, honey, and sugar) is prepared, with each ingredient being associated with a specific deity (Ambikā, Gaṇāmbikā, Gaṅgā, Gaurī, Manonmanī) who is invoked and worshipped.

sections.content: [This section describes the preparation for the ceremonial bath (snapana) of the deity. It involves setting up a sacred space (sthaṇḍila), arranging pots (kalaśas) filled with scented water, and consecrating them by invoking Śiva, the five mūrtis (Īśāna, etc.), and the eight Vidyeśvaras. The priest performs mudras and chants mantras to imbue the water with divine power before the bath begins.]
sections.summary: Snapana refers to the ceremonial bath for the deity. This section details the preparations, which include creating sacred diagrams (sthaṇḍilas) and arranging one, nine, or more consecrated pots (kalaśas). These pots are filled with water and other sacred substances, adorned, and divinized by invoking various forms of Śiva and other deities into them. The priest chants mantras like the Prāsāda mantra and Gaurī Gāyatrī extensively to sanctify the water, making it fit for the divine bath.

sections.content:
VIII ātmārcana (regarding oneself as the very deity, eschewing the notion that he is mere man)
सामान्यार्घ्यतोयेनास्त्रमन्त्रेण स्वशिरसि सम्प्रोक्ष्य स्वासने ॐ हां शिवासनाय नमः। इति पुष्पं दत्वा । हृदये-ॐ हां हं हां शिवमूर्तये नमः। इति मूर्ति विन्यस्य। ललाटे-हरिश्चन्दनेन तिलकं कृत्वा । शिरसि ॐ हां हौं शिवाय नमः। इति पुष्पमारोप्य आत्मनि पशुबुद्धिं त्यक्त्वा शिवोऽहमिति भावयेदित्यात्मार्चनम्।।
sections.summary: Ātmārcana is the ritual where the priest identifies with the deity. By sprinkling himself with consecrated water, placing flowers on his seat, heart, and head with specific mantras, and applying a tilaka, he meditatively discards the notion of being a mere human ('paśu-buddhi') and assumes the consciousness of being one with Śiva ('Śivo'ham').

sections.section_title: Mantra-śuddhi and Saurārādhana (Worship of the Sun)
sections.content: [Section XI describes Mantra-śuddhi, the purification of the primary mantras by chanting them slowly three times. Section X then details Saurārādhana, the worship of the Sun god (Śiva-Sūrya). This is a complete sub-ritual with its own saṅkalpa, nyāsa, dhyāna, āvāhana, āvaraṇa pūjā (worship of attendant deities in concentric circles), and offerings.]
sections.summary: This section covers two distinct but related preliminary rituals. First, Mantra-śuddhi involves purifying the main mantras to be used in the worship by chanting them systematically. Second, Saurārādhana is the detailed worship of the Sun, viewed as a form of Śiva (Śiva-Sūrya). This includes specific hand gestures (nyāsa), meditation verses (dhyāna śloka), invocation, and a three-tiered enclosure worship (āvaraṇa pūjā) for the Sun's attendant deities, planets, and guardians of the directions. It concludes with offerings and a prayer to Tejaścaṇḍa.

sections.section_title: Preliminaries: Worship of Gaṇeśa and Door Deities
sections.content: [This part begins the second major sequence of the worship. (a) It details the worship of Gaṇeśa to ensure the successful completion of the main Śivārcanā. This involves saṅkalpa, detailed nyāsa using Gaṇeśa's bīja mantras and Vedic hymns, and worship of his attendant deities. (b) It is followed by Dvāra-yajana, the worship of deities at the sanctum door, including Gaṇapati, Sarasvatī, Mahālakṣmī, Nandi, Mahākāla, and others, to gain permission to enter.]
sections.summary: The second sequence starts with preliminary worship. First, a detailed worship of Gaṇeśa is performed to remove any obstacles to the main Śiva pūjā. This includes invoking Gaṇeśa and performing extensive body-mantra placements (nyāsa) and enclosure worship (āvaraṇa pūjā). Following this is the Dvāra-yajana, or worship of the deities guarding the sanctum door. The priest invokes and worships figures like Nandi, Mahākāla, Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and the door guardians (dvārapālas) before entering the sanctum proper.

sections.section_title: Elimination of Obstacles and Entering the Sanctum
sections.content: [Subsections (c) and (d) describe Vighnodvāsana and Yavanikotsāraṇa. The priest ritually removes three kinds of obstacles (celestial, terrestrial, interpatial) using mantras and mudras, accompanied by the ringing of a bell. He then draws aside the curtain (yavanikā) covering the sanctum, meditating on the deity Sthāṇu, and formally requests permission from Vṛṣabha (Nandi) to proceed with the worship.]
sections.summary: This part details the final steps before beginning the worship of the main Liṅga. The priest performs Vighnodvāsana to eliminate the three types of obstacles, using mantras, mudrās, and ringing the temple bell to announce the commencement of divine rites. He then performs Yavanikotsāraṇa, the ritual drawing aside of the curtain, and enters the sanctum after seeking permission from Vṛṣabha (Nandi) and meditating on the Astra-rāja (king of divine weapons) who guards the threshold.

sections.content: [This section focuses on the worship within the sanctum. It starts with (a) Liṅga-śuddhi: cleaning the main deity. The priest first worships the pedestal (āsana), then removes the previous day's decorations (nirmālya) and places them aside for Caṇḍeśvara, and washes the Liṅga and pīṭha. This is followed by (a) Āvaraṇārcana: worship of the enclosure within the sanctum (garbhagṛha), including Vāstubrahman, Gaṇapati, Mahālakṣmī, Sarasvatī, the seven Gurus, and the nine Śaktis at the gomukha.]
sections.summary: The worship now moves to the main deity. It begins with Liṅga-śuddhi, the cleaning of the Śiva Liṅga. The priest worships the divine seat (Dharmāsana, etc.), ceremonially removes the previous night's offerings (nirmālya), and cleans the Liṅga. This is followed by Āvaraṇārcana, the worship of the deities residing within the sanctum's enclosure, such as Vāstu Brahman, Gaṇapati, Mahālakṣmī, Sarasvatī, the lineage of Gurus, and the nine Śaktis, establishing a divine protective space.

sections.content: [(d) Śivāsanārcanā: pīṭha-pūjā and nyāsa. This is a highly detailed and esoteric part of the worship, focusing on the consecration of the deity's seat (pīṭha/āsana). The priest mentally constructs the seat layer by layer, starting from the Ādhāraśakti at the bottom, through various deities, tattvas (principles), and cosmic planes, culminating in the divine lotus upon which Śiva will be invoked. This involves extensive nyāsa and worship of numerous minor divinities that constitute the divine throne.]
sections.summary: This section describes the intricate worship of Śiva's seat (Śivāsana). It's a complex visualization and ritual where the priest mentally constructs the divine throne layer by layer. Starting from the base power (Ādhāraśakti), he worships Ananta and other nāgas, the Dharma and Adharma quadrants, the seats of Yoga and Siṃha, the cosmic lotus with its stalk and petals, and the mandalas of the Sun, Moon, and Fire. On this fully constructed divine seat, he establishes the different Tattvas (Ātma, Vidyā, Śiva) and performs nyāsa for the five faces of Sadāśiva, preparing for the main invocation.

sections.section_title: The Arcana Proper: Invocation and Offerings
sections.content: [This section details the main part of the worship. (a) Āvāhana (Invocation): The priest, through yoga and mantra, draws the divine consciousness of the formless, all-pervading Paraśiva down into the prepared Liṅga, making the form manifest for worship. This is a highly spiritual process involving prāṇāyāma, mudrās, and intense visualization. (b) Pādya, etc.: The priest offers water for washing the feet (pādya), hands (arghya), and sipping (ācamana) to the now-present deity. (c) Abhiṣeka (Ritual Bath): This is the central ritual bath of the deity with various prescribed substances like oil, pañcagavya, pañcāmṛta, fruit juices, scented water, etc., each accompanied by specific mantras. The section ends with post-bath rituals like drying, dressing, and applying sacred unguents.]
sections.summary: This is the climax of the pūjā. It begins with Āvāhana (Invocation), where the priest uses yogic techniques and mantras to draw the formless supreme Śiva into the physical Liṅga, using various mudrās (sthāpana, sannidhāna, etc.) to establish and fix the divine presence. After the invocation, basic hospitalities are offered (pādya, arghya, ācamana). The central act of Abhiṣeka (ritual bath) is then performed, an elaborate anointing of the Liṅga with numerous substances like oil, milk, curd, honey, fruit juices, coconut water, and finally pure water, all while chanting Vedic hymns and Āgamic mantras. Following the bath, the deity is adorned with clothes, sacred thread, perfumes, flowers, and bilva leaves.

sections.content: [After the decoration, the priest worships the deity with the eight sacred names, the aṣṭamūrti forms, and various lists of names (aṣṭottaraśata, triśata, sahasranāma). He offers incense (dhūpa) and light (dīpa). This leads into a detailed āvaraṇa pūjā, or enclosure worship, where all the attendant deities surrounding Śiva in his celestial court are worshipped in concentric circles or specific locations around the main Liṅga.]
sections.summary: After the Abhiṣeka and Alaṅkāra, the priest performs arcana (worship with flowers) using various sets of names for Śiva: the eight primary names, the Aṣṭamūrti names, 108 names (aṣṭottaraśata), and Sahasranāma (1000 names). This is followed by the detailed Āvaraṇa Pūjā (enclosure worship). In a series of concentric circles (āvaraṇas), the priest worships Śiva's immediate attendants: his five faces with their Śaktis, his limbs (aṅgas), the Vidyeśvaras, Gaṇeśa, the Lokapālas (guardians of the directions), and their weapons.

sections.content: [This section describes the worship of the three principal Śaktis: Yoga-śakti, Bhoga-śakti, and Vīra-śakti. Their locations are defined: Yoga-śakti is on the left side of the Liṅga or identified with the pedestal itself; Bhoga-śakti is the metallic icon kept near the Liṅga for enjoyment; Vīra-śakti is a separate, four-armed deity in an outside shrine. The text provides detailed procedures, including dhyāna ślokas and āvaraṇa pūjās, for Bhoga-śakti and Vīra-śakti.]
sections.summary: The worship continues with the three forms of the Goddess (Śakti). Yoga-śakti is worshipped as the inherent power within the pedestal. Bhoga-śakti, the consort icon for enjoyment, is worshipped next to the Liṅga with her own āvaraṇa pūjā. Finally, Vīra-śakti, a powerful, four-armed form housed in a separate shrine, is worshipped. Her worship is a complete ritual in itself, involving nyāsa, dhyāna, abhiṣeka, and a five-tiered āvaraṇa pūjā with various attendant goddesses and deities.

sections.content: [This part covers the worship of the wider circle of deities and concluding rituals. Parivārārcana is the worship of attendant deities in their respective shrines around the temple. Agni-kārya is the daily fire ritual (homa) performed in the yāga-śālā. Bali-haraṇa is the ceremonial offering of food portions (bali) to all the deities of the temple, including guardians and elemental spirits, carried out in a procession around the temple.]
sections.summary: This section details the concluding rituals of the daily worship cycle. Parivārārcana involves worshipping all the attendant deities (parivāra devatās) in their respective shrines within the temple complex. This is followed by Agni-kārya, the mandatory daily fire ritual (homa or havana) conducted in the yāgaśālā according to prescribed procedures. Finally, Bali-haraṇa, the ceremonial distribution of food offerings (bali) is performed. The priest takes a portion of the main offering in a procession around the temple, giving a share to all the deities, guardians, and spirits residing in the temple premises.

sections.section_title: Final Rites: Pādukā-pūjā, Caṇḍikeśvara Worship, and Śayanotsava
sections.content: [The final part of the daily worship. Pādukā-pūjā is a brief worship of the sacred sandals of the processional icon. The priest then transfers the nirmālya (used items from the main worship) to the shrine of Caṇḍikeśvara, who is considered the steward of Śiva's property, and performs his worship. The chapter concludes with a description of śayanotsava, the final nightly ritual where the processional deity (as Umā-Maheśvara) is taken in a procession to a special swing or bed in the śayana-mandira (sleeping chamber) and put to rest for the night with offerings and lullabies.]
sections.summary: This details the final acts of the day. Pādukā-pūjā is the worship of the holy sandals where the processional icon is kept. The priest ritually hands over the 'merit' of the day's worship to Śiva. This is followed by the worship of Caṇḍikeśvara, where the nirmālya (remains of the main offering) is given to him. The elaborate morning worship is contrasted with briefer afternoon (mādhyāhnika) and evening (sāyampūjā) services. The day concludes with Śayanotsava, where the processional deity and consort are taken to a sleeping chamber, placed on a swing, offered milk and other items, and ritually put to bed.

chapter_summary: Chapter II, 'Nityārcanā in Śiva Temples', provides a detailed, step-by-step account of the standard daily worship procedure (Nityārcanā) performed in South Indian Śiva temples, based on various Śaivāgama texts. The chapter meticulously outlines the entire cycle of rituals, beginning with the priest's entry and purification rites (ātma-śuddhi, bhūta-śuddhi, antaryāga). It then describes the main Prātaḥ-kāla-pūjā (morning worship), centered around the abhiṣeka (ritual bath) and alaṅkāra (decoration) of the Śiva Liṅga, followed by an intricate āvaraṇa pūjā (worship of attendant deities). The chapter also covers the worship of the Sun (Saurārādhana), Gaṇeśa, and the three principal forms of Śakti (Yoga, Bhoga, Vīra). It concludes with the daily fire ritual (Agni-kārya), the distribution of food offerings (Bali-haraṇa), and the final night ceremony (Śayanotsava) where the processional deity is put to rest. The text is rich with Sanskrit mantras, dhyāna ślokas (meditation verses), and detailed procedural instructions, offering a comprehensive manual for Śaiva temple worship.
key_arguments: The daily worship in Śiva temples is not a simple act but a highly structured, complex, and systematic procedure derived from authoritative Āgama texts.
The ritual process emphasizes purification at all levels—personal, material, spatial, and elemental—as a necessary prerequisite for divine communion.

Worship is multi-layered, involving not just the main deity but a whole pantheon of attendant deities (parivāra), guardians (dvārapāla), and divine principles (tattvas), reflecting a complex theological and cosmological framework.
The priest's role transcends that of a mere functionary; through rituals like Ātmārcana and Antaryāga, the priest is required to achieve a state of identification with the divine (Śivo'ham).
The ritual cycle encompasses the entire day, with specific worship sequences prescribed for different times (kāla-pūjā), culminating in the Śayanotsava, which mirrors human daily rhythms.
key_takeaways: Nityārcanā is the foundational daily ritual in a Śiva temple.

The core components of the worship include purification (śuddhi), invocation (āvāhana), ritual bathing (abhiṣeka), decoration (alaṅkāra), offerings (naivedya), and worship of attendant deities (āvaraṇa pūjā).
Internal, mental worship (Antaryāga) and self-identification with the deity (Ātmārcana) are as crucial as the external, physical rituals.
Key figures worshipped alongside Śiva include Gaṇeśa (for removing obstacles), Kṣetrapāla (guardian of the site), Caṇḍikeśvara (steward of offerings), and the various forms of Śakti.
The entire temple space is considered sacred and alive, with specific rituals like Bali-haraṇa meant to propitiate all divine beings residing within the premises.

historical_figures.name: Talakādu Kṛṣṇa-Dīkṣita
historical_figures.significance: Edited the 'Arcanāprakāśa' (published 1962), the primary source compilation for the procedure described in this chapter.

historical_figures.name: Śiva
historical_figures.significance: The central deity to whom the Nityārcanā is offered.

historical_figures.name: Gaṇeśa
historical_figures.significance: Worshipped at the beginning of rituals to remove obstacles.

historical_figures.name: Durgā
historical_figures.significance: Worshipped at the main door along with Gaṇeśa.

historical_figures.name: Kṣetrapāla
historical_figures.significance: Guardian of the temple grounds, whose permission is sought before worship.

historical_figures.name: Caṇḍikeśvara
historical_figures.significance: An important devotee of Śiva who receives the 'nirmālya' (remains of worship).

historical_figures.name: Naṭarāja
historical_figures.significance: The iconic representation of Śiva worshipped during pradośa-pūjā.

historical_events.significance: The source text compiled by Talakādu Kṛṣṇa-Dīkṣita, upon which this chapter's description of Nityārcanā is based, was published by Manonmani-granthamālā.

geographic_locations.context: The chapter explicitly states that the described procedure is a standard one adopted in the Śiva-temples in South India.
geographic_locations.significance: This grounds the ritual practice geographically, indicating its prevalence in the Dravidian temple tradition which is heavily influenced by the Āgamas.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: The title of the chapter and the main subject, referring to the regular, daily ritual sequence in a temple.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: Traditional doctrine or precept, a collection of sacred writings
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: The primary textual source for the worship procedures, such as Kāmika Āgama.
The officiating priest who performs the worship.
The pedestal, usually outside the main shrine, where offerings (bali) are placed for attendant deities.
The ceremonial flag-post located in the temple courtyard.
The image of the crouching bull, Nandi, Śiva's vehicle and devotee.
The icons of guardian deities flanking the entrance to the sanctum.
A mantra used for protection, purification, and opening locks.

sanskrit_hindi_terms.translation: mixture of the five products of the cow
sanskrit_hindi_terms.context: A purifying mixture of milk, curds, ghee, urine, and cowdung, used for cleaning and consecration.
The flowers, garlands, and other items from the previous day's worship, which are removed before the new worship begins.
The initial set of rituals for the priest to purify his own body and mind.
A yogic and meditative ritual to purify the five elements (bhūtas) within the priest's body.
A mental worship where the entire ritual is visualized and performed internally.
The ritual cleaning and consecration of all vessels and materials to be used in the worship.
The main ritual bath of the deity with various sacred liquids.
Synonym for Snapana, the act of anointing and bathing the deity.
The central act of invoking the divine presence into the idol or liṅga.
The systematic worship of attendant deities who reside in concentric circles (āvaraṇas) around the main deity.
The ritual procession to distribute food offerings (bali) to all the secondary deities and spirits in the temple complex.
The final ritual of the night, where the processional deity is ceremonially put to rest.

quotations.quote: ॐ भद्रं कर्णेभिः श्रुणुयाम देवा भद्रं पश्येमाक्षभिर्यजत्राः । स्थिरैरङ्‌गैस्तुष्टवांसस्तनूभिः व्यशेम देवहितं यदायुः ॥
quotations.context: Recited by the priest as he enters the main door of the temple.
Recited by the priest to open the door of the sanctum.

quotations.quote: स्वामिन् सर्वजनान् भूमौ रक्षितुं क्षेत्रपालक। शिवपूजाविधानार्थे मुद्रादण्डं प्रदेहि मे ॥
quotations.context: A prayer asking Kṣetrapāla for the 'mudrādaṇḍa' or permission to conduct the worship.

quotations.quote: वेदान्तवेद्योऽखिलविश्वमूर्ते विभो विरूपाक्ष विशेषवेद्य। विश्वेश्वराशेषविशेषमूर्ते कवाटमुद्घाटय कालकाल ॥
quotations.context: Recited to request Śiva to 'open the door' of the sleeping chamber of the processional deity.

quotations.quote: अन्तर्यागं ततः कुर्याद् हृदये च विधानतः। नाभौ होमविधानेन ललाटे ध्यानयोगतः ।।
quotations.context: A verse describing where internal worship (antaryāga) is to be performed: in the heart, navel (as fire-ritual), and forehead (as meditation).

quotations.quote: आगमार्थ तु देवानां गमनार्थं तु रक्षसाम्। कुर्वे घण्टारवं तत्र देवताह्वानलाञ्छनम्।।
quotations.context: A verse explaining the purpose of ringing the bell: to invite the gods and drive away malevolent spirits.

quotations.quote: वक्रतुण्ड महाकाय सूर्यकोटिसम्प्रभ । अवघ्नि कुरु मे देव पूजाकार्येषु सर्वदा ॥
quotations.context: A common prayer to Gaṇeśa asking him to remove obstacles from the worship.

alternative_viewpoints.viewpoint: Variations in who performs the cleaning of the sanctum.
alternative_viewpoints.context: According to Śaivāgama-sāra, the priest himself must clean the sanctum. However, Kāmikāgama allows the priest's attendant (paricāraka) to clean the area up to the bali-pīṭha.

alternative_viewpoints.viewpoint: Variations in the frequency of daily worship.
alternative_viewpoints.context: Worship can be done three times (morning, noon, night), six times (ṣaṭ-kāla-pūjā), two times (day and night), or just once at noon, according to different textual prescriptions.
